vignette:
Mateo sits in my office with the ramrod posture of a man who has spent three decades commanding respect. At 55, he is a Captain in the Navy, a man whose presence is meant to project calm authority. His uniform, when he wears it, is impeccable, the creases sharp, the brass polished. But in the civilian clothes he wears to our sessions, he seems adrift, the structure that has defined his life now a poor shield for the chaos within.

His story doesn’t begin on the deck of a destroyer, but in the sun-drenched market of his family’s hometown, a place he hadn’t visited in years. It was five years ago. He was on leave, a rare chance to shed the weight of command and simply be a son, a cousin, a man among his people. He remembers the smell of roasting corn and the cacophony of vendors hawking their wares. He was haggling over the price of a handmade leather belt, laughing with the shopkeeper, when the world dissolved into a concussive roar.

The car bomb detonated less than a hundred yards away. Mateo, a man trained to react to explosions with tactical precision, was thrown to the ground like everyone else. For a moment, there was only a high-pitched ringing and a thick, choking cloud of dust that tasted of pulverized concrete and something acridly chemical. When he could see again, the vibrant market was a monochrome scene of carnage. His training kicked in, a desperate, automatic response. He began to triage, to apply pressure to wounds, to shout orders that no one heard or heeded. But he was not Captain Rivera here. He had no crew, no corpsman, no authority. He was just a man in a civilian shirt, kneeling in rubble, surrounded by the dead and dying. The helplessness was a poison, seeping into him with every scream he couldn't soothe and every life he couldn't save.

He returned to duty a week later, burying the experience under layers of protocol and routine. He told himself it wasn't his battle, that he was a bystander, a victim like any other. But the Captain’s mind, trained for total situational awareness, had recorded everything in excruciating detail.

Now, years later, the market is never far away. A car backfiring on the street outside his naval base apartment sends a jolt of pure adrenaline through him, his heart hammering against his ribs as if trying to escape. He finds himself scanning rooftops and parked cars when he walks with his partner, Sofia, his hand reflexively hovering near his lower back, where a sidearm would be. She asks him what’s wrong, why he’s so tense, and he dismisses it as “the job.”

He no longer goes to crowded restaurants. The overlapping sounds of conversation, the clatter of plates, the sudden laughter—it all feels threatening, a prelude to chaos. He insists on sitting with his back to a wall, his eyes constantly sweeping the room, assessing threats that aren't there. Sofia has learned to stop suggesting they go to concerts or festivals.

The nights are the worst. Sleep offers no refuge, often jolting him awake in a cold sweat, the scent of dust and cordite still thick in his nostrils. He sees the face of a young girl whose hand he held as she bled out on the cobblestones, her eyes wide with a question he could not answer. The guilt is a constant, heavy anchor. He, the commander of a warship, a man responsible for hundreds of lives, had been powerless to save just one.

He finds himself irritable and distant, snapping at junior officers for minor infractions, then retreating into a stony silence. The easy camaraderie he once had with his crew is gone, replaced by a chasm of experience he cannot share. Sofia tells him he feels far away, even when he’s sitting right next to her. He looks at his own hands, the hands that have guided vessels through treacherous waters, and sees only their failure in that dusty, blood-soaked market square. The Captain is still on duty, but the man is lost somewhere in the wreckage.
